definition: MCP restrictions control which tools and data sources an AI assistant is allowed to use. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard way tools get plugged into assistants; restrictions decide, per person or per role, which of those plugs are live. An engineer might get the deploy tool; support staff don't.

edges.label: limits
edges.note: Restrictions decide which tools the loop may call on each lap.

example.body: A company wires its codebase, docs, and deploy pipeline into an AI assistant. Engineers get all three. Support staff get docs only — the deploy tool simply doesn't appear for them. Same assistant, same model, different keys. When leadership asks “could the AI push bad code to production?”, the answer lives in these restrictions, not in the model.
example.title: The deploy button test

footnotes.body: In practice this means an MCP server registry with per-role allowlists, enforced by the harness at tool-call time — often bound to corporate identity (e.g. Okta OIDC) with role switching. Claude Desktop's historically coarse MCP control is the cautionary tale: convenient, but hard to govern.
footnotes.label: For the technical reader

name: MCP Restrictions
tagline: Rules about which tools an AI assistant may touch — and which roles get which tools.
whyItMatters: This is where AI governance gets concrete. Without restrictions, every assistant has every tool — convenient until someone asks it to do something it shouldn't be able to. Restrictions are how companies give AI real power without giving it the keys to everything.
